newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Controversial Michael Collins film opens in Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Michael Collins film opens in Ireland.

text.p: "Michael Collins", which opened in Ireland on Wednesday evening, looks set to break local box office records while debate swirls over its account of the struggle for independence and the bitter internal conflict that followed.
Collins, an IRA guerrilla commander, masterminded the fight against British rule, negotiated the peace treaty of 1921 and was assassinated the following year.
The $28 million Hollywood-backed epic claimed best film and best actor awards at the Venice film festival but has provoked fierce criticism in Britain and Ireland.
"Back to the Future it may be; history it ain't," Paul Bew, a leading Irish historian, wrote in Britain's Daily Telegraph.

Writer-director Neil Jordan has also been accused of inflaming passions at a sensitive time in the Northern Ireland peace process. The IRA bombed the British army's headquarters in Northern Ireland last month, bringing war to the province after a two-year respite.
But Jordan, whose previous films include "Interview with the Vampire" and "The Crying Game", has defended his work.
"It's not a work of history, it's not a historical document...The film is as accurate a dramatic reconstruction as I could make," he told an Irish film magazine.
Jordan has also been criticised for his harsh portrayal of Eamon de Valera, who served as Irish prime minister and president for decades.

Sile de Valera, granddaughter of de Valera and an Irish opposition politician, has said she is worried about "the way the film seems to try to portray "Dev' as someone that was trying to set up Michael Collins for the ambush in which he died. All of that is outrageously untrue."

Arriving for the Dublin premiere, Jordan denied implicating de Valera in Collins death. "It's a kind of controversial history and I would have been very surprised if I had made a film that nobody objected to," he told reporters.

Liam Neeson, the "Schindler's List" star who plays Collins, also attended the irish opening, as did U.S. ambassador to Ireland, Jean Kennedy Smith, who has a cameo role in the film and Irish justice minister Nora Owen, one of Collins' grandnieces.
Owen, who is involved in current talks on the future of Northern Ireland, rejects criticism that the film promotes violence.
"It does not glorify violence and to anybody working and living in the North now who would choose to say it in some way supports a violent campaign, I have to say that is not the case."
The film opens in 120 cinemas across Ireland from Thursday.

"If interest before it opens is an indication of how it will do, there will be full houses everywhere," said Ita Bourke of Ward Anderson which runs a number of Irish cinemas. "It will probably be the biggest thing ever."
